Skinny Skyscrapers New York

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...a South African who is helping to change the skyline of New York

Unique Selling Point:
Chris Shirley is a South African who works as a design engineer in New York and he has been involved with a large engineering firm that designs most of the the new buildings in New York. They were involved with the new World Trade Center and several of the highest buildings in the city. Some of the new high rises are "skinny buildings" and apartments in these buildings go for in excess of $100 million! Chris shows us around.

Summary:
Chris Shirley is a South African who works as a design engineer in New York and he has been involved with a large engineering firm that designs most of the the new buildings in New York. They were involved with the new World Trade Center and several of the highest buildings in the city. Some of the new high rises are "skinny buildings" and apartments in these buildings go for in excess of $100 million! Chris shows us around.

Further information:
Chris Shirley is a South African who works as a design engineer in New York and he has been involved with a large engineering firm that designs most of the the new buildings in New York. They were involved with the new World Trade Center and several of the highest buildings in the city. Some of the new high rises are "skinny buildings" and apartments in these buildings go for close to $100 million! We fist contacted Chris last year, but only managed to film everything earlier this years. Chris took is to several of the buildings he was involved in, including World Trade Center Building number 7 and a new hotel building that is part of the complex. He took us to the 69th story and we had unique views of Manhattan. Chris has a interesting story to tell and has interesting knowledge of the new type of "skinny buildings" that is springing up everywhere. His personal pet project is the highest building in Manhattan which is also a skinny building and where apartments will cost between $50 mil and $100 mil -- it is called 432 Park Avenue. And most of the apartments have been sold long before completion. Chris also has interesting stuff about "air rights" in New York that allows developers to buy air space from land owners and this enables them to build higher than ever before. It is an interesting story about a South African who is working on the tallest buildings in the world, and it gives one a rare view of Manhattan as well.

Accommodation in New York, 2 nights 2x $135 Transport costs $55 S&T $160 (2 x $80)

Press Release:


Carte Blanche visits the Big Apple for stunning views from new so-called skinny buildings where an apartment will set you back a cool $50 to $100-million. We meet South African design engineer Chris Shirley, a man integral to several of these New York high-rise apartment buildings and who is taking the investment world by storm.

Script:


V/O:
This man in a South African living in New York. He is on his way to work. His name is Chris Shirley and he is a structural engineer.

At the moment he has three babies in his life. This is what little Nicholas and Mila look like. And this is Chris’ third baby…… 432 Park Avenue. He calls this building his baby because he designed its structure. It is the tallest apartment building in the Western hemisphere and is part of a new wave of New York skyscrapers now transforming the Big Apple’s skyline.
Chris:
New York is open for development. It is a city that adds the amount of Skyscrapers in one year that San Francisco has in total.
LINK:
To put this in perspective, one must realise that San Francisco is the 13th biggest city in the US.
V/O:
The city has a considerable number of tall office and residential buildings.

In New York the building boom has changed the skyline of the city radically.

The Twin Towers once stood here. Now the site boasts a new World Trade Center complex and its enormous Freedom Tower.

And the iconic Empire State building has been surpassed in height by 432 Park Avenue.

Design engineers are crucial in building these skyscrapers.
Chris:
We’ll design the building, the skeleton of the building to resist the forces that are applied to it and the architect will obviously come up with the overall shape, the design, what it looks like.
V/O:
Chris works for a company called WSP and they are involved in designing and building some of the tallest structures in the world.

After graduating from Wits University Chris worked for a South African company that was bought out by WSP and suddenly he found himself part of a global firm. He applied to go to New York.
Chris:
And I was not going to stay for too long. A couple of months but this couple of months kind of turned into years and I am still here. You know, eight years on, so…
LINK:
Working for this company Chris soon became involved in some of the most important building projects in New York City, including the new World Trade Center complex.
Chris:
My company was involved in Tower 1, Tower 2, Tower 3 and the memorial. The design of the memorial. ….. and the memorial. Three thousand people lost their lives there and when you go there, it’s definitely, your walking in an area that is hallowed ground. So it kind of adds to the importance of the work that we do there.
V/O:
It is a spectacular site with impressive structures. One of them is 30 Park Place.
Chris:
30 Park Place is a gorgeous building that we designed. And I was heavily involved with. It rises over nine hundred feet high. Just in comparison that is taller than the Hillbrow Tower by a good thirty, forty meters. And 30 Park Place is the kind of residential tower of the WTC site.
V/O:
This representation of what the whole complex will look like when complete, shows that the building is much slimmer than those around it.

Chris took us up in the construction elevator to the sixty third floor to show us the structural design.
Chris:
The basic system is a concrete core in the centre that rises through the building.
V/O:
Once on the 63rd floor we see the building’s central core. This whole floor is destined to become four separate apartments.

The views are spectacular.

There is also an interesting view down to an older building that was once the tallest building in the world – 40 Wall Street.

On other floors the interiors are taking shape. The finishes are impressive.

This is the view from one of the living rooms in the unfinished apartments. At these heights your nearest neighbour is the Freedom Tower.
Chris:
In terms of the buildings, there is a race for height in general whether it is office or residential. But specifically in the residential market height is definitely a driving force. Developers want to get as high as they can go. You have amazing views of the city but it also becomes very expensive. Those apartments, some of them sell up to 90 million dollars.
V/O:
It’s hard to ignore the fact that in New York the really tall buildings are getting skinnier and narrower than ever before.
LINK:
And that is because of a peculiar building regulation in New York in New York City.
V/O:
This regulation deals with so-called property air rights.
Chris:
What happens is that with the sort of restrictions on zoning in the city you have very specific what we call FAR, which is floor area ration. The developers can maximize that FAR ratio and make these skinny, slender towers versus sort of lower rise buildings.
LINK:
This is how it works. If the floor-area ratio in your area is say 15, it means you can build a 15 story building on your plot of land. However, if you use half the space, your building can be 30 stories high. And if you make it even skinnier, you can add another 15 stories. And if you use a tiny piece of land to build on you can go really high but then your building becomes even skinner.
Chris:
These guys are building, especially developers, they are building in a very small portion of their site and this height can be really increased by this ratio to be super skinny and slender.
V/O:
This is a time-lapse of construction at four-thirty-two Park Avenue. The building took more than 2 years to complete and soon the remaining windows will be fitted.

It topped out at just over four hundred and twenty five metres…..
LINK:
However, the site’s own air rights were not enough to allow them to build to that that staggering height.
Chris:
And to add to that height they buy the additional air rights of the building surrounding it. So that also adds to this FAR
V/O:
432 Park Avenue bought out the air rights belonging to surrounding buildings. This enabled them to build so high and so skinny.

This artist’s impression shows what the interior of the apartments will look like once completed. The penthouse apartment takes up the whole floor and will sell for a cool hundred million dollars.

But such tall buildings bring other challenges, especially when it comes to wind.
Chris:
Wind is the driving factor that we design for, basically high rise buildings. They are clever ways to design around wind. If you look at the Burj Khalifa, there are no straight edges on that building. It is all circular so the wind can kind of find its way around those areas easier.
LINK:
But 432 Park Avenue has square angles. To counter the force of the wind, Chris came up with a novel solution.
Chris:
When we ran the wind tunnel studies at 432, we found that there was a lot of drag on the building from wind. So to reduce that we have these sort of open floors where there are no windows in. Basically the wind is allowed to pass through and this happens at five locations and reduces the wind drag on the building quite significantly and proves the overall building performance.
V/O:
432 Park Avenue is just the start of the new generation of super skinny buildings that will give the New York Skyline an entirely new appeal. And, Chris will remain key to developing many of them.
Chris:
That is why I kind of became an engineer. It was that appeal to see something that is truly amazing. Hopefully a hundred years from now, similarly the way we look at the Chrysler Building, and think like ‘Wow that building is amazing, I wonder how it was built and who did it?’ Hopefully people will do the same for my buildings and that is kind of special.
